title: Vesper and the Visitor
premise: Folklorist Isandro Vasquez arrives in the dying village of Vesper to record songs no one will sing twice, and discovers they are fragments of a sealing ritual performed by the town's founders two centuries ago. When an excavation crew unearths a door sealed from the inside, the thing behind it begins finishing the founders' work in reverse, claiming villagers one memory at a time — including Isandro's own past, which she has been documenting to keep from forgetting. To stop it she must complete the ritual herself, but the final verse requires a willing sacrifice of everything she loves, and the village's last founder-descendant, Mateo, is both her only ally and the price. Isandro sings the closing verse alone, trading her recorded life for the village's future, and the door reseals with her on the inside; Mateo survives, carrying her notebooks as the only proof she ever existed.
about_author: Cyrus Voss is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing oral histories in remote mountain communities before turning to fiction. Their work explores what records can hold and what they inevitably fail to save.

chapters.title: The Songs They Won't Sing Twice
chapters.summary: Isandro arrives in Vesper with recording equipment and a grant deadline, interviewing elderly residents about local ballads. Every singer stops mid-verse at the same line and refuses to continue, some visibly frightened. POV: Isandro. Emotional beat: scholarly curiosity curdling into unease as she realizes the silence itself is a pattern.

chapters.title: A Village That Forgets on Purpose
chapters.summary: Isandro digs through the church archive and finds hymnals with pages razored out and parish registers with names inked over. The priest, Father Anselm, warns her gently that some things were removed so they could stay removed. POV: Isandro. Emotional beat: the thrill of a researcher finding deliberate erasure — evidence someone wanted this buried.

chapters.title: Mateo of the Founders' Line
chapters.summary: Isandro tracks down Mateo Reyes, last descendant of the founding families, who lives outside town and refuses to speak with her until he hears her play back a fragment of the forbidden song. Something in his garden dies overnight after the recording plays. POV: Mateo. Emotional beat: reluctant recognition that the outsider has already gone too far to turn back.

chapters.title: What the Excavation Uncovered
chapters.summary: A road crew blasting for a reservoir cuts into the old quarry and exposes a stone door fitted seamlessly into bedrock — its hinges on the inside. Workers report humming from behind it. The foreman orders concrete by morning. POV: foreman Delia Cruz. Emotional beat: practical denial cracking against something that should not have hinges where it does.

chapters.title: Sealed From Within
chapters.summary: Isandro photographs the door and matches its carved markings to the torn hymnal pages: the missing verses are inscribed there, worn as if touched by generations of hands. Father Anselm sees her photos and goes gray, telling her the founders sang themselves hoarse to close it. POV: Isandro. Emotional beat: dread of understanding — the songs aren't folklore, they're instructions.

chapters.title: The First Verse Returns
chapters.summary: That night every radio in Vesper plays static shaped like singing. Old Tomás, the first villager who refused to sing for Isandro, is found standing at the quarry at dawn with no memory of the last forty years. POV: Tomás. Emotional beat: terror of self-erasure, the horror of being hollowed from the inside out.

chapters.title: Documentation Is a Kind of Prayer
chapters.summary: Isandro realizes her recordings of the partial verses slow the thing's advance — Tomás stabilizes when she plays them beside him. She begins transcribing obsessively, sleeping three hours a night. Mateo starts helping her despite himself. POV: Isandro. Emotional beat: purpose hardening into obsession; the first warmth between her and Mateo.

chapters.title: The Crew That Wouldn't Leave
chapters.summary: Delia refuses to abandon the contract; the company sends more workers. Two men pry at the door's edge and find it warm. By evening one is reciting the second verse perfectly in a voice not his own, and the door's seal cracks a finger's width. POV: Delia. Emotional beat: guilt and helplessness as corporate stubbornness feeds the thing.

chapters.title: Hymns for a Hungry Door
chapters.summary: The possessed worker sings the second verse fully and collapses; the village loses its well water, which runs black and tastes of iron. Mateo reveals the founders' bargain: the door was sealed from within by a volunteer who stayed behind. POV: Mateo. Emotional beat: inherited shame — his family built the cage and abandoned the key.

chapters.title: Anselm's Confession
chapters.summary: Father Anselm admits the Church has known for generations; his predecessor's letters describe each reopening and the verse-by-verse re-sealing, always ending with someone staying. He gives Isandro the founders' original score, incomplete at the final movement. POV: Anselm. Emotional beat: the collapse of institutional protection — faith kept the secret but never solved it.

chapters.title: Memory Debt
chapters.summary: Villagers begin losing specific memories — faces, first loves, their children's names — in the order the verses were originally sung. Isandro discovers her own childhood memories slipping, replaced by pages she never wrote. POV: Isandro. Emotional beat: intimate horror; the enemy is editing her from within her own head.

chapters.title: The Third Verse, Sung Wrong
chapters.summary: Desperate, the village attempts the third verse communally in the church. It works — then falters when half the singers forget the words mid-line, and the backlash kills the oldest choir member. POV: choir leader Rosa. Emotional beat: grief and fury; collective courage isn't enough when memory itself is the weapon.

chapters.title: Quarantine
chapters.summary: Delia seals the quarry road and calls authorities, who arrive, investigate, and leave with a report calling it gas leaks. The company plans to entomb the site — which Mateo knows will only trap the pressure until it bursts. POV: Delia. Emotional beat: bitter clarity that institutions protect themselves, not people; justice won't come from above.

chapters.title: What Isandro Forgot
chapters.summary: Mateo finds Isandro's earliest notebook and reads aloud the life she's losing — a sister, a fire, a promise — while she listens like a stranger. She chooses to record her own memories as ammunition against the erosion. POV: Mateo. Emotional beat: love declared sideways, through preservation rather than words.

chapters.title: The Fourth Verse Demands a Name
chapters.summary: Deciphering the score, Isandro learns each verse must be sung by a named descendant of a founder — and only Mateo's bloodline remains. The entity begins whispering his name through the cracked door, offering to release the village if he comes willingly. POV: Mateo. Emotional beat: the corruption of power inverted — temptation dressed as mercy.

chapters.title: Rosa's Bargain
chapters.summary: Rosa proposes tricking the entity: sing the fourth verse in Mateo's name but channel it through the whole village, diluting the claim. The attempt partially succeeds — the crack seals halfway — but the entity takes Rosa's voice permanently as payment. POV: Rosa. Emotional beat: defiant sacrifice; the village learning to fight together outside any law or church.

chapters.title: The Night of Open Doors
chapters.summary: The entity retaliates: doors throughout Vesper stand open at dawn though all were locked, and everyone who slept near an open door wakes without their past week. Panic erupts; families flee. POV: multiple villagers, braided. Emotional beat: communal breaking point — the choice between flight and standing ground.

chapters.title: The Final Movement
chapters.summary: In the founders' score, Isandro finds the fifth verse's requirement hidden in musical notation: it must be sung by someone who stays behind willingly, giving the door their whole remembered life. She tells no one. POV: Isandro. Emotional beat: quiet resolve beneath heartbreak; love against duty resolved by choosing both.

chapters.title: Everything I Recorded
chapters.summary: Isandro spends her last day copying her notebooks to Mateo, dictating memories of her sister and the fire, kissing him once at the quarry fence. She lies about the plan; he suspects and lets her go. POV: alternating Isandro and Mateo. Emotional beat: devastating tenderness — goodbye disguised as housekeeping.

chapters.title: The Closing Verse
chapters.summary: At moonrise Isandro enters the gap in the door and sings the fifth verse from inside, feeding it her memories verse by verse as the entity consumes them. The door grinds shut on her final note. Outside, the black water clears; Tomás remembers his wife. POV: Isandro, dissolving. Emotional beat: transcendence through sacrifice — documentation becoming literal prayer.

chapters.title: Aftermath: The Man Who Remembers Her
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Vesper heals; the company abandons the site; Delia resigns. But Mateo retains every memory of Isandro — the entity took her life, not others' knowledge of it — and he reads her notebooks aloud to the village so she isn't erased twice. POV: Mateo. Emotional beat: grief transformed into custodianship.

chapters.title: Coda: A Song Sung Twice
chapters.summary: Years on, Mateo teaches the completed ritual-song to the village children, sung openly now, twice and more. At the quarry's concrete cap, faint through the stone, a new melody answers his — hers, patient, keeping the door company. POV: Mateo. Emotional beat: bittersweet peace; love outlasting duty, memory outlasting death.
